title: Dealing With Feeling Crowded on Public Transport: The Potential Role of Design
research_question: To estimate the buffering role of design resources (seat demarcation, window permeability, outdoor surrounding) in both subjective experience (crowding, pleasantness, stimulation, dominance) and behavioral responses (patterns of eye movements) to crowded conditions on a bus, and to assess how these physical attributes interact to explain changes in emotional responses and perceived crowding.

participants.description: Phase 1: 80 students (35% female, aged 23.71 years, SD = 3.29) from a university in northern Italy. Phase 2: 33 graduate students (11 males, 22 females, aged 24.86 years, SD = 3.02) enrolled in a university in northern Italy.
participants.recruitment: Phase 1: snowball sampling. Phase 2: volunteered to participate.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 18 virtual simulation images (Autodesk 3DS Max®) depicting a spatially uncomfortable social situation on a bus with one intruder. Images varied across three factors: (a) seat demarcation (poor, moderate, well-demarcated), (b) window permeability (low, high), and (c) outdoor surroundings (traffic congestion, urban environment, rural landscape).

mechanisms: Redirection of attention away from aversive social stimuli (passenger) to restorative elements (rural landscape, window views) or compensatory indoor elements (seat demarcation).
Environmental features (seat demarcation, window permeability, outdoor surroundings) act as coping resources or buffers against crowding.
Restorative environments (urban/natural landscapes) make negative social stimuli less threatening.

Compensatory effect: when one environmental attribute is poorly supportive (e.g., poor seat demarcation, obstructed window, stressful outdoor view), attention shifts to other available supportive elements (e.g., window, rear windows, seat demarcation itself).
Increased sense of control through well-defined spatial boundaries and access to information about the outside world.
moderators: Outdoor surrounding (traffic congestion, urban environment, rural landscape)
implementation_implications: Design of public transit vehicles should consider gradients of protective physical attributes (e.g., type of physical barrier) rather than just presence/absence of amenities.
Stronger barriers between seats may be needed to facilitate adjustment to crowding and increase passengers' sense of control.
Rethink spatial organization of public transportation to consider the outdoor environment as a primary factor affecting travel experience.
For urban buses on traffic roads, prioritize indoor design elements that increase control (e.g., seat demarcation) over larger windows that expose to stressful surroundings.
For routes through attractive urban areas (e.g., historical heritage), increase access to the outdoor environment (e.g., larger windows).

limitations: Reliance on a single-item self-reported measure of perceived crowding, which may have low reliability and decrease statistical power.
Potential compositional biases in eye-tracking data due to the central position of the passenger in the images.

Use of static images as experimental stimuli may be challenging for simulating social interaction and personal space invasion, which ideally requires multiple sensory proxies (tactile, olfactive, acoustic).
The experience of adverse reactions on a crowded bus can only be approximated by simulations, requiring further validation studies.
The study did not consider the gradient for window permeability, suggesting future research could explore different levels.
The manipulation check for outdoor surroundings used only 'being away' from ART, not other restorative qualities like fascination.
The study's participants were university students, potentially limiting generalizability to older populations or those with different cultural backgrounds or stressor familiarity.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Dealing With Feeling Crowded on Public Transport: The Potential Role of Design
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Extensive evidence has documented the moderating role of design attributes in crowding; yet, the effect of public transportation design on travel experience has been overlooked. We conducted a within-design experimental study aimed to estimate the buffering role of design resources in both subjective experience (crowding, pleasantness, stimulation, and dominance) and behavioral responses (patterns of eye movements) to crowded conditions on a bus. Three physical bus elements (seat demarcation, access to the window, outdoor surrounding) and their degree of supportiveness (poor, moderate, high) were manipulated. The results of Phase 1 ( N = 80) and Phase 2 ( N = 33) confirmed the beneficial moderating effect of the three physical components on crowding and their compensatory role. The adopted multimethodological approach confirmed to be an ecologically valid strategy for studying the effects of the physical environment on human behavior. Practical implications and directions for future research are discussed.
